findings.lesson_text: Some of Antony's funeral speech is almost directly lifted from North's translation, showing how closely Shakespeare worked from this source.
findings.issue: The lesson claims Antony's funeral speech is 'almost directly lifted' from North's Plutarch translation. Scholarly consensus holds the opposite: in Plutarch (both North's translation and the Greek original), the speeches of Brutus and Antony at the funeral are only briefly summarised, not given in full. Shakespeare therefore composed the 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' oration largely from scratch. Research indicates the speeches draw more on Appian's Roman history than Plutarch, and neither source provides a detailed funeral oration to 'lift' from. The error risks misleading students who are asked to comment on Shakespeare's use of his source material.
findings.canonical_truth: Plutarch's Lives (including North's 1579 translation) summarises the funeral in a few lines without reproducing the speeches verbatim. Scholars identify Appian's Roman history as the closer source for elements of Antony's funeral oration. Shakespeare largely invented the rhetorical content of both Brutus's and Antony's speeches. The broader claim that Shakespeare used North's Plutarch as a primary source for the play's plot and characters is accurate; the specific claim that the funeral speech was 'almost directly lifted' is not supported by the text.

findings.lesson_text: In Act 1, Scene 2, he reveals in soliloquy that he will throw forged letters through Brutus's window, written 'in several hands' (different handwriting) as if from multiple Roman citizens begging Brutus to act against Caesar.
findings.issue: The lesson attributes the forged-letters plan to a soliloquy at the end of Act 1 Scene 2. However, the plan is actually carried out in Act 1 Scene 3, where Cassius instructs Cinna to throw letters 'in at his windows' and to set other papers in locations where Brutus will find them. Cassius's soliloquy closing Act 1 Scene 2 is about exploiting Brutus's 'honourable mettle' — it alludes to writing letters but the full plan and instruction to Cinna happens in the next scene. The lesson's act/scene attribution for the forged-letters revelation is therefore slightly imprecise.
findings.canonical_truth: At the end of Act 1 Scene 2, Cassius's soliloquy indicates he will write letters to Brutus 'in several hands as if they came from several citizens' (paraphrase). The actual staging of this plan — where Cassius tells Cinna to 'throw this in at his window' — occurs in Act 1 Scene 3 (lines 142–160 in Folger). Students citing the plan should reference both scenes accurately.

findings.lesson_text: Key Fact: Cassius uses three key tactics: flattery ('many of the best respect in Rome' look to Brutus), belittlement of Caesar (the Tiber story, Caesar's fever in Spain), and an appeal to Brutus's ancestry (his ancestor Lucius Junius Brutus expelled the last Roman king).
findings.issue: The lesson lists the appeal to Brutus's ancestry as one of Cassius's three spoken tactics in Act 1 Scene 2. In the play, the explicit invocation of 'Junius Brutus' as an ancestor appears in the forged letters Brutus reads in Act 2 Scene 1 ('Shall Rome, etc.… Brutus thou sleep'st: awake, and see thyself'), not in Cassius's direct speech in Act 1 Scene 2. Cassius does allude to the name 'Brutus' and Roman republican spirit, but the Lucius Junius Brutus ancestry argument is associated with the letters' content and Brutus's own reflection in Act 2. Cassius in Act 1 Scene 2 focuses on the Tiber story and the star/underlings speech. Attributing the ancestry appeal as a direct spoken tactic of Cassius in Act 1 Scene 2 is imprecise.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 1 Scene 2, Cassius's persuasion relies on: (1) flattery of Brutus's reputation, (2) the Tiber swimming story belittling Caesar, (3) Caesar's fever in Spain, and (4) the 'fault is not in our stars' speech. The Lucius Junius Brutus ancestry reference is found in the letters Brutus reads in Act 2 Scene 1 and in Brutus's own references to his family name — it is not one of Cassius's explicitly stated spoken arguments in Act 1 Scene 2.

findings.lesson_text: Antony agrees to his own nephew's execution without hesitation: 'He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him.'
findings.issue: The lesson describes this as Antony spontaneously agreeing to condemn his nephew, presenting it as an act of cold initiative. In the actual scene (Act 4 Scene 1), it is Lepidus who raises Publius as a condition — he says 'Upon condition Publius shall not live, / Who is your sister's son, Mark Antony' — i.e. Lepidus is forcing Antony's hand as part of a trade. Antony's line 'He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him' is therefore a grudging concession to Lepidus's demand, not an unprompted act of ruthlessness. The lesson's framing that Antony 'agrees without hesitation' (implying he volunteers this) obscures the dramatic context in which Lepidus extracts the concession.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 4 Scene 1, the proscription scene opens with the three men already ticking off names. Lepidus raises the condition 'Upon condition Publius shall not live, / Who is your sister's son, Mark Antony' — meaning Lepidus will allow Antony's other relatives to be sacrificed only if Antony condemns his own nephew too. Antony's reply 'He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him' is a concession to this trade. The moment still shows ruthlessness, but it is also a moment of coercion and political bargaining rather than pure unprompted callousness.

findings.lesson_text: Cassius orders his servant Pindarus to kill him with the same sword that killed Caesar
findings.issue: The lesson says Cassius orders Pindarus to kill him with 'the same sword that killed Caesar.' In the actual text (Act 5 Scene 3, Folger and MIT editions), Cassius asks Pindarus to strike him with 'the same sword' that ran through Caesar — but crucially, this is presented as poetic irony: 'Caesar, thou art revenged / Even with the sword that killed thee.' The phrase refers to the same sword Cassius personally used in the assassination. This point is handled adequately by the lesson's own next sentence, but the initial framing 'the same sword that killed Caesar' implies Pindarus uses an identifiable murder weapon, whereas it is Cassius's own sword (which he used in the assassination) — not, for example, a sword literally taken from Caesar's body.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 5 Scene 3, Cassius (believing Titinius has been captured) asks Pindarus to 'guide thou the sword' into his own chest. His final words 'Caesar, thou art revenged / Even with the sword that killed thee' confirm that the sword is the one Cassius used to stab Caesar in Act 3 — i.e. Cassius's own weapon, not something literally borrowed from Caesar's corpse. The lesson's description is close to accurate but could be read as implying a different prop.

findings.lesson_text: Calpurnia has a prophetic dream of Caesar's statue 'like a fountain with an hundred spouts' running blood
findings.issue: The lesson paraphrases Calpurnia's dream with the phrase 'running blood.' The actual text of Act 2 Scene 2 reads 'like a fountain with an hundred spouts / Did run pure blood' — the key word 'pure' is omitted from the lesson's paraphrase. While this is minor and the paraphrase is broadly accurate, students quoting the lesson's version for analysis would be using an incomplete version of the quotation. The word 'pure' has interpretive weight: blood described as 'pure' introduces an ambiguity (Decius later reinterprets it as life-giving rather than deadly), and its omission removes a detail relevant to AO2 language analysis.
findings.canonical_truth: Act 2 Scene 2: Caesar reports Calpurnia's dream — 'She dreamt tonight she saw my statue, / Which like a fountain with an hundred spouts / Did run pure blood; and many lusty Romans / Came smiling and did bathe their hands in it.' The key phrase is 'run pure blood' (not simply 'running blood'). Decius's reinterpretation exploits the word 'pure' to suggest the statue represents Caesar giving reviving sap/blood to Rome.

findings.lesson_text: He speaks with quiet authority ('I was born free' echoes Cassius, but from a position of legitimate power).
findings.issue: The lesson claims Octavius 'speaks with quiet authority' and that something he says echoes 'I was born free.' However, the phrase 'I was born free as Caesar; so were you' is Cassius's line from Act 1 Scene 2 — Octavius never utters or paraphrases it. The parenthetical implies Octavius mirrors this sentiment 'from a position of legitimate power,' but no such line or echo exists in the text attributed to Octavius. The lesson appears to construct a thematic parallel that has no textual basis in Octavius's actual dialogue.
findings.canonical_truth: The line 'I was born free as Caesar; so were you' belongs exclusively to Cassius (Act 1 Scene 2). Octavius's lines in the play are few; he asserts authority by disagreeing with Antony's military dispositions (Act 5 Scene 1: 'I do not cross you; but I will do so') and by giving the closing order for Brutus's honourable burial (Act 5 Scene 5). None of his lines echo or reference the 'born free' phrasing. The implied parallel is not supported by the text.

findings.lesson_text: Antony, finding Brutus's body, delivers the play's final verdict: 'This was the noblest Roman of them all. / All the conspirators, save only he, / Did that they did in envy of great Caesar; / He only, in a general honest thought / And common good to all, made one of them.'
findings.issue: The lesson quotes only the first five lines of Antony's tribute and presents them as the 'final verdict.' The speech in fact continues: 'His life was gentle, and the elements / So mixed in him that nature might stand up / And say to all the world, \"This was a man.\"' The omitted lines are arguably the most celebrated and analytically rich part of the speech: the 'elements so mixed' metaphor (humoral theory, Renaissance concept of the ideal human) and the culminating 'This was a man' are key evidence for the theme of Brutus as the ideal Roman and for AO3 (Elizabethan views on the balanced, virtuous man). Stopping the quotation early and calling it 'the final verdict' misleads students into thinking the speech ends there.
findings.canonical_truth: Antony's full tribute in Act 5 Scene 5 reads: 'This was the noblest Roman of them all. / All the conspirators save only he / Did that they did in envy of great Caesar. / He only in a general honest thought / And common good to all made one of them. / His life was gentle, and the elements / So mixed in him that nature might stand up / And say to all the world "This was a man."' The final two lines are essential for high-level AO2 and AO3 analysis.
